title: Weak Squares
subtitle: A square only stays weak as long as no pawn can ever attack it again
summary: A square becomes permanently weak the moment no pawn of its own color can ever defend it again — pawns only move forward, so the damage cannot be undone. This lesson shows the classic d5 hole from a Sicilian-style structure: White plants a knight there, and Black, lacking any pawn lever and any minor piece that can reach it, can never evict it.

rootAnnotations.title: What makes a square 'weak'
rootAnnotations.body: A square is weak — not merely undefended for the moment, but weak — when no pawn of its own side can ever again guard it. A misplaced piece can be reorganized; a pawn that is gone or has moved past a square cannot un-move. That irreversibility is the entire concept.
Look at Black's pawns before White's first move: the c-pawn is gone from the board entirely, and the e-pawn already stands on e5. Which Black pawn could ever challenge a white piece landing on d5?

rootAnnotations.title: Permanent vs temporary weakness
rootAnnotations.body: A square defended by a piece is only temporarily weak — trade or drive off that piece and the defense can return one day. A square whose only possible pawn-defenders are gone or have advanced past it is permanently weak: for the rest of the game, nothing but another piece can ever contest it. This is why players call it a 'hole,' not a 'gap.'

annotations.title: The knight claims the hole
annotations.body: White's c3-knight jumps straight into d5. Compare the Sicilian Defense lesson: Black's own ...e5 push is exactly what carved this hole, trading dynamic central play for a permanent structural concession — 'a hole White will try to own with a knight forever,' as that lesson puts it. Here is the moment that debt comes due. The pawn on e4 defends d5, so the knight isn't just uncontested — it's protected too.

annotations.title: The only try
annotations.body: No black pawn can touch d5 — the c-pawn is off the board and the e-pawn stands past it on e5. The only remaining option is to attack the knight with a piece instead, rerouting the d7-knight toward f6, where it eyes d5 from the far side.

White is glad to trade. Removing the challenger costs Black a knight of its own, and the weakness of d5 is completely untouched by the swap — the square doesn't become less weak just because nothing currently sits on it.

annotations.title: The hole outlives the piece
annotations.body: Even with no White piece sitting on d5 right now, the square is still permanently weak — nothing stops White from returning a rook, a queen, or another minor piece there later, helped along by the half-open c-file this same structural imbalance created. A weak square is a standing invitation, not a one-time visitor.

annotations.title: What you should have noticed
annotations.body: Three recognition cues: a pawn move that passes a square and leaves no sibling pawn behind to defend it creates a permanent hole, not a temporary one; a piece posted on such a square can be traded off, but the square itself cannot be un-weakened, since pawns cannot move backward; and weak squares just in front of a fixed pawn chain — here Black's own d6–e5 chain — are the single most reliable landing pads for enemy minor pieces in all of chess.
